newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Case crumbling as smiling Malan awaits verdict.
newsitem.headline: Case crumbling as smiling Malan awaits verdict.

text.p: The prosecution case in South Africa's biggest apartheid-era "dirty war" trial collapsed further on Friday with the acquittal of two more co-defendants accused with former defence minister Magnus Malan.
The two, a former special operations major and a security police colonel, were accused of the 1987 death squad massacre of 13 blacks in KwaMakhuta near the Indian Ocean port city of Durban.

The judge had yet to rule on the charges against Malan, the most senior apartheid-era leader to be tried for atrocities. South Africa does not operate a jury system. Rulings are made by a judge in consultation with two assessors.

Malan appeared buoyed by the acquittal a day earlier of six policemen charged in the killings. On Friday, he greeted the six on his way in, waved and gave a thumbs-up sign to crowds gathered outside the colonial-style courthouse.

In the building he and the remaining defendants -- a top Inkatha official, three generals, one major, a vice-admiral and a brigadier, joked with members of the crowded gallery, saying they had plenty of free seats in the dock now.
"We have found no proof of express authorisation of the KwaMakutha incident...or tacit approval (by the military)," Judge Jan Hugo told the court.

The state had tried to show the accused organised the attack as part of a covert defence force operation using the mainly Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party against the then-banned African National Congress of Nelson Mandela.

Judge Hugo, who on Thursday strongly criticised the prosecution case, told the court that much of the documentary evidence dealt with a paramilitary force set up under Malan to help Inkatha leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi.
But Hugo said the documents made no implication that this meant a death squad, adding that crucial to the state's case was the term "offensive" unit, found in many of the documents.
It often seemed to have a "innocent" meaning, in that it did not mean death squads, but a security function, he added.

Thursday's acquittals sparked speculation that Malan would also walk free -- a verdict which some political analysts said would further damage the public's shaky faith in the South African justice system.
The six cleared on Thursday were policemen in the KwaZulu black homeland run by Buthelezi until it was scrapped after all-race elections in April 1994.
Inkatha hailed their acquittal as "a triumph of justice".
"The state should in future be more prudent and cautious before embarking on prosecutions which are widely perceived to have high-level political connotations," it said in a statement.
But Mandela's ruling African National Congress called the verdict a travesty.

"In the eyes of the our people, the prosecution team failed them. This will have far reaching consequences. It is doubtful whether our people will ever have confidence in the judicial system if it remains the same," the ANC said.

Senior members of the movement have previously lamented the fact that most of South Africa's judges are white men appointed during the apartheid era, and have accused some of them of administering racially-biased justice in the past.
